name: Superposition Explained
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Both, Not Either: Understanding Superposition
lesson.summary: Explains what superposition really means as a physical state rather than hidden classical uncertainty, using interference and a worked Hadamard gate example.
lesson.body:
The previous section described a qubit's state as alpha|0⟩ + beta|1⟩. Superposition is the name for this combined state, and it is worth being precise about what it does and does not mean. It does not mean the qubit is secretly a 0 or secretly a 1 and we simply have not looked yet, the way a coin under a cup has already landed heads or tails even before you lift the cup. A qubit in superposition is, before measurement, genuinely neither state alone. Its description requires both amplitudes together, and experiments involving interference (discussed below) confirm that this is a real physical distinction, not just a statement about our ignorance.

The key difference between superposition and ordinary classical uncertainty is interference. Classical probabilities are always non negative and simply add up: if there is a 30 percent chance of rain and a 70 percent chance of no rain, those possibilities cannot cancel each other out. Quantum amplitudes are complex numbers, and complex numbers can partially or fully cancel when combined, a phenomenon called destructive interference, or reinforce each other through constructive interference. This is what gives quantum computation its distinctive character: a well designed quantum algorithm arranges for the amplitudes of wrong answers to interfere destructively and cancel, while the amplitudes of the right answer interfere constructively and grow.

A concrete example makes this precise. The Hadamard gate, one of the most common single qubit operations, transforms |0⟩ into the equal superposition (1/√2)|0⟩ + (1/√2)|1⟩. If you then apply the Hadamard gate a second time to that same state, you do not get some new, more scrambled superposition. You get back |0⟩ exactly. This happens because applying the gate to each term produces a |1⟩ component with amplitude +1/2 from the first term and -1/2 from the second term, and these two contributions cancel exactly, while the |0⟩ components add constructively. That precise cancellation is interference in action, and no classical probability distribution behaves this way.

An analogy, and it is only an analogy, is two water waves overlapping in a pool. Where a crest meets a crest, the water rises higher than either wave alone; where a crest meets a trough, the water can go flat. Quantum amplitudes combine in a mathematically similar way when quantum states overlap, which is why physicists sometimes describe quantum mechanics as a theory of interfering waves of probability. The analogy breaks down if pushed too far, since qubit amplitudes are complex numbers governing discrete measurement outcomes rather than a continuous physical medium, but it captures the intuition of constructive and destructive combination reasonably well.

Superposition scales dramatically with more qubits. Two qubits together can be in a superposition of all four combinations, |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, and |11⟩, and in general n qubits can be placed in a superposition spanning 2 to the power n basis states at once. This exponential growth in the size of the description is often, and misleadingly, summarized as a quantum computer trying every answer simultaneously. The truth is more subtle and more interesting: a superposition over many possibilities is only useful if you can also engineer the interference that concentrates amplitude onto the answer you actually want, since a plain measurement of an unstructured superposition just returns one random basis state. That subtlety, and how it connects to entanglement, is the subject of the next two sections.
